title: How to Buy Property in Cyprus: Step-by-Step Guide and Due-Diligence Checklist (2026)
subtitle: From reservation to title deed, and what to check before you pay

intro: Buying property in Cyprus follows eight steps in a fixed order, and the order is what protects you. The paperwork is routine. Losses come from a step that was skipped or done late: a lawyer chosen by the seller, a contract never lodged at the Land Registry, a defects list never written down. All figures are as of October 2026.

sections.heading: How to buy property in Cyprus: eight steps in order, with typical timing

blocks.text: EU citizens buy on the same terms as Cypriots. Non-EU citizens, including British buyers since Brexit, need permission from the Council of Ministers (step 7). Foreign-ownership rules were under review in 2026, so confirm the current position with your lawyer before buying land or more than one property.

items.title: Fix your budget and prove your funds
items.text: Assemble passport, proof of address and bank statements showing where the money came from before you wire anything. Typical time: 1-6 weeks.

items.title: Appoint your own lawyer
items.text: Independent of the seller and the developer, and before you reserve anything. The fee is usually 1% plus VAT. Typical time: a few days.

items.title: Reserve the property
items.text: A written reservation agreement takes the unit off the market. The fee is roughly €3,000-€10,000; agree in writing what is refunded if due diligence finds a defect. Typical time: 1-3 days.

items.title: Run due diligence
items.text: Your lawyer checks title and registered charges, the seller's right to sell, permits and unpaid municipal charges. Typical time: 1-3 weeks.

items.title: Sign the sale contract
items.text: Standard developer contracts favour the seller, so your lawyer negotiates changes. The deposit is commonly 20-40% on a resale. No stamp duty applies to contracts signed from 1 January 2026. Typical time: weeks 3-6.

items.title: Lodge the contract at the Land Registry
items.text: Within 6 months of signing, for a €50 fee. It gives you an enforceable right to be registered as owner, even if the seller becomes insolvent or sells the unit twice. Get written confirmation.

items.title: Obtain permission (non-EU buyers only)
items.text: Your lawyer files the Council of Ministers application right after signing. No government fee. Typical time: weeks to months.

items.title: Pay the balance and transfer title
items.text: Resale: you pay the balance and the transfer fee, currently €8,600 on a €300,000 resale after the 50% reduction. New-build: VAT is invoiced instead and no transfer fee applies. A resale typically takes 2-4 months from signing (indicative).

blocks.title: Lodge the contract in the first week
blocks.text: The legal window is 6 months, and there is no reason to use it. Lodging in the first week protects you for the whole period in which something could go wrong.

blocks.text: New-builds are often sold before individual title deeds exist. The land is first registered as one plot, and separate deeds follow after completion, final approvals and the registration of each unit, with no universal timeframe. A missing deed is common and is no automatic warning sign; judge the project by its permits, its progress and the developer's record.

One thing does hold a deed up. If the developer borrowed against the land, the Land Registry cannot issue individual deeds to buyers until that charge is released. The unit is then yours in practice and not yet on paper, which blocks a mortgage and complicates a sale.

sections.heading: How to check the developer and the project before you pay

blocks.text: The title search, permits and contract belong to your lawyer. Judging the company belongs to you. A building can match the brochure and still leave you in difficulty if the developer's finances fail.

blocks.title: Ask the developer before paying a reservation fee
items: On your last three completed projects, were individual title deeds issued to buyers, and how long did it take from handover?
Is a mortgage or charge registered over this land, and what does the contract say about releasing it from my unit?
What is the contractual completion date, and what happens if it is missed?
Is the payment schedule tied to calendar dates or to construction milestones?
Do you hold the building permit and, for finished projects, the certificate of final approval?

blocks.title: Verify independently
items: Your lawyer requests the search certificate for the plot and reads every registered charge.
Deeds issued on past projects are public record at the Department of Lands and Surveys, so the answer can be checked.
Visit a development finished three to five years ago and speak to residents.

blocks.title: Red flags
blocks.text: Pressure to pay a reservation fee before your lawyer has seen anything. Payments tied to dates instead of building stages. Steering towards a specific lawyer. Vague answers about deeds on past projects. A price well below comparable nearby projects.

sections.heading: Off-plan payments and deposit protection in Cyprus

blocks.text: Cyprus does not mandate performance guarantees on off-plan purchases. Safeguards exist, and each one has to be written into the contract. Until handover your money is with the developer unless an escrow arrangement is agreed.

blocks.title: Typical off-plan instalments on a €300,000 price (excluding VAT)
rows: On signing the contract (25%)
Stage payments during construction (45%)
On completion and handover (30%)
blocks.note: Market range: 20-30% on signing, 40-50% in stages, 20-30% at handover. VAT is added: €15,000 at the reduced 5% rate if you qualify, €57,000 at the standard 19% rate.

head: Safeguard
What it does
Position in Cyprus
rows: Milestone-linked instalments
You pay when frame, roof or fit-out is verifiably reached
Negotiate it and name who certifies, ideally an independent surveyor
Bank guarantee or performance bond
Covers deposit and instalments until title is delivered
Not a legal requirement; ask for it in the contract
Escrow account
Payments go to a third party and are released at milestones
Not compulsory; some developers offer it
Contract lodged at the Land Registry
Enforceable right to registration, also against a double sale
Within 6 months of signing; the most valuable single step

blocks.title: Clauses to negotiate in an off-plan contract
items: A firm completion date plus a long-stop date after which you may rescind and recover your deposit in full
Liquidated damages for delay beyond a defined grace period
A defects liability period of at least 24 months from handover, including structural and waterproofing defects
A bank waiver letter or a binding timetable to discharge the developer's mortgage before handover
A specification of materials and finishes, with remedies for deviation

blocks.text: If the developer becomes insolvent, a lodged contract gives you an enforceable right to registration, a stronger position than an ordinary creditor. A bank guarantee covers the payments you made. With neither, you join the queue of creditors, and those processes take years and rarely pay out in full.

sections.heading: Snagging and handover: inspecting a new-build before the final payment

blocks.text: The final instalment is your moment of most leverage: the developer wants it and you have not yet paid it. Holding part of it back until a defects list is cleared is common, but Cyprus has no mandatory handover procedure with automatic retention rights. The right to inspect and to retain a defined sum has to be in the contract before you sign.

blocks.title: Handover inspection checklist
items: Waterproofing and damp: roofs, terraces, balconies, window and door edges
Tiling and finishes: uneven or hollow-sounding tiles, grouting, paint
Electrical: every socket and switch tested, the consumer unit, extractor fans
Plumbing: every tap and drain, water pressure, leaks, hot water at every outlet
Doors, windows and joinery: all open, close and lock squarely
Villas: pool and pump, external drainage, boundary walls
Specification: finishes, fittings and layout match the contract

items.title: Photograph and describe
items.text: Photograph and date every defect and list the items room by room.

items.title: Get written acknowledgement
items.text: The developer acknowledges the list in writing and agrees a time frame for repairs.

items.title: Tie the retention to the list
items.text: State which items must be cleared before which part of the retained sum is released.

items.title: Re-inspect before paying
items.text: Verify the repairs yourself or through your surveyor before you release the retained amount.

blocks.title: Buying from abroad
blocks.text: Use an independent snagging surveyor who acts for you. Sources give the warranty periods for hidden defects inconsistently, so confirm the periods in your own contract with your lawyer.
